title: the dice game
hook: on the road home, Duryodhana tells Shakuni what is eating him, and Shakuni offers a way to win without a war
carry: name the sting before it becomes a plan

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dice game began without dice: Duryodhana fooled by Maya's hall, and laughed at. Did you help before you laughed? Day seven hundred sixty-five.

Duryodhana is heading home to Hastinapura, and he keeps sighing. His uncle Shakuni, riding with him, notices and asks what's wrong. And Duryodhana tells him. Not a polite version. The whole thing. In the poem, he pours it out: the kings bowing to his cousin, the wealth flowing in, the hall that made a fool of him, the laughter. He says he can't bear it. He says it's burning him up inside. Today, a confession on the road, and the uncle who hears in it an opportunity.
screen: `SIGHING ON THE ROAD HOME.` → `SHAKUNI ASKS.` → `THE WHOLE THING POURS OUT.`

segments.voice: Listen to what Duryodhana actually says. He doesn't say the Pandavas cheated. He doesn't say they wronged him. He says they're prospering, and he can't stand it. Their success is the injury. That's envy in its plainest form, and the poem lets him say it out loud, without dressing it up. Shakuni listens. Then he does what a good friend might do, at first. He tells Duryodhana not to grieve, that the Pandavas have their good fortune and he has his. But Duryodhana won't be comforted. So Shakuni changes course. You can't beat them in battle, he says, in effect. They're too strong. But there's another way. Yudhishthira loves to play dice, and he doesn't play well. I do. Invite him to a game, and I'll win everything he has, and you won't have to lift a weapon. Sit with how clever that is, and how dark. A war would be open. Everyone would see who attacked whom. A game is different. It looks friendly. It has rules. The loser agreed to play. Shakuni is offering Duryodhana a way to take a kingdom and keep his hands clean. And notice who starts this. Not a monster from a cartoon. A hurting man, and an uncle who knows exactly where it hurts. The dice game is born on this road, out of envy spoken aloud and a plan offered in reply.
screen: `THEIR SUCCESS IS THE INJURY.` · `SHAKUNI TRIES COMFORT FIRST.` · `YUDHISHTHIRA LOVES DICE.` · `A WAR THAT LOOKS LIKE A GAME.` · then, large: `ENVY SPOKEN, A PLAN OFFERED.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow, and let the face soften. Is there anyone whose good fortune is hard for you to watch right now? A friend's news, a colleague's win, a sibling's easy road. You don't have to say it out loud. Just let the name come, and notice the sting, honestly, the way Duryodhana did. Then breathe out slowly, and let the sting be just a sting, not a plan. If you pray, you can bring that person's good fortune into your prayer. If not, simply let the breath carry the sting a little further off. The bell holds the time.
Envy, taking someone else's good fortune as your own wound. Today, Duryodhana speaks it aloud on the road home, and Shakuni answers with a plan to win a kingdom without a war.
Your line: name the sting before it becomes a plan. Today, if someone else's good news stings, name the sting to yourself before anyone hands you a plan. Day seven hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: In Hindu retellings of the Mahabharata, Shakuni is known as the master of the dice, and the conversation on the road is told as the moment Duryodhana's envy becomes a plan.

myth: Duryodhana claimed the Pandavas had cheated him
he said their prosperity itself was what he couldn't bear.
Shakuni first told Duryodhana not to grieve
he tried comfort before he offered the plan.
Shakuni proposed attacking the Pandavas in battle
he said they were too strong to beat that way, and offered dice instead.

fork.setup: you're Shakuni. your nephew is consumed by envy of cousins too strong to defeat in war. what do you offer him?
options: a game of dice, with you playing.
fork.reveal: he tries comfort first, then offers dice: Yudhishthira loves the game and plays badly, and Shakuni plays well.

original.note: Sanskrit akṣa: a die, one of the dice used in the game.

trapdoor: what you thought: a friendly game that went wrong.
what it means: a plan born from envy, offered by Shakuni as a way to take a kingdom without a war.
what a scholar hears: Shakuni's plan depends on the look of fairness, since a loser who agreed to play cannot easily call it an attack.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Duryodhana confesses his grief to Shakuni; Shakuni proposes the dice game)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm that Duryodhana confides in Shakuni on the way back, naming the Pandavas' prosperity and the humiliation in the hall.
In Ganguli, Duryodhana also speaks of wishing to end his life; this script deliberately softens that to 'burning him up inside' and does not mention self-harm.
Confirm that Shakuni first consoles him, then says the Pandavas cannot be defeated in battle, and proposes dice because Yudhishthira is fond of the game but unskilled while Shakuni is skilled.
Original: akṣa (a die) is offered from general Sanskrit; confirm it is the term used in the dice-game section or set to null.
The trapdoor's third floor is the script's reading; a Keeper may refine.

Editor pass: replaced the stock 'quiet. Too quiet.' with the text's own detail (Duryodhana sighing, which is what Shakuni asks about); cut 'and they have Krishna' from Shakuni's paraphrase, since the cited speech is about the Pandavas' strength; replaced the cliché 'villain twirling a mustache'.
Audit (2026-10-01): checked the road conversation (Shakuni consoles first, says battle won't work, proposes dice) against Ganguli's Dyuta Parva; no change needed.
